title: OpenHOI: Open-World Hand-Object Interaction Synthesis with Multimodal Large

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract and contribution list claim 'state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods by a large margin,' while Section 4.3 states that the results 'show marginal improvements in some metrics, though differences are within standard deviations reported by prior works' and that the approach has 'competitive performance but not a definitive advantage.' These claims are mutually contradictory; the conclusion is overstated relative to the paper's own evaluation.

The text says the method's differences from baselines are 'within standard deviations reported by prior works,' but Tables 2 and 3 show much larger differences. For example, GRAB seen MPJPE is Ours 47.64±1.03 vs Text2HOI 56.29±2.13, and FID is 26.43±0.77 vs 33.72±1.27. These differences are not within the reported standard deviations, so the narrative misstates the table results.

The 'Unseen' split is not a strict unseen-object test: the paper states 'the unseen testing set includes object instances and categories potentially overlapping with training, limiting strict unseen generalization claims.' Yet the tables label this split 'Unseen' and the paper uses it to support open-world generalization claims.

The reverse update is written as X_{t-1} = μ_t + σ_t ε, with σ_t defined as ((1-ᾱ_{t-1})/(1-ᾱ_t)) β_t. That quantity is the posterior variance; the standard deviation is its square root. Thus the noise term should be √σ_t ε, or σ_t should be defined as the square root. Using the variance as the noise scale is mathematically incorrect.

The table marks HOIGPT as possessing '3D MLLM,' but the text describes HOIGPT as a 'pure LLM architecture' that 'lack[s] grounding in actual 3D perception or reasoning.' HOIGPT is not a 3D multimodal LLM, so the table misattributes this capability.

The ablation text says removing affordance causes 'minor degradations' and the physical-refinement losses provide 'incremental' improvement, then immediately claims 'Without this guidance, the diffusion model exhibits two key failure modes... fails to generate complete long-horizon HOI sequences' and produces 'physically unrealistic results.' Table 4 shows only modest differences, so the paragraph is self-contradictory and overstates the ablation findings.

It says 'During sampling, we apply classifier-free guidance by randomly substituting 10% of conditioning inputs with unconditional noise while retaining 90% of the original conditions.' Conditional dropout for classifier-free guidance is performed during training (as correctly stated in Section 3.2), not during sampling. This is a corrupted protocol description.

The paper defines SmoothRate = dFID/dt and says 'dt is the derivative of time.' FID is a distributional distance between sets of motions, not a time-dependent signal, so this derivative is undefined and cannot measure temporal smoothness. The reported SmoothRate values are therefore not a valid metric.

The authors say they performed paired two-sample t-tests 'repeating each test five times and reporting the mean p-value.' Averaging p-values across repeated runs is not a valid statistical procedure: it ignores dependence among repetitions and can misrepresent significance. A proper combined analysis or reporting of all repetitions is required.

The table is titled 'Two-test Statistically Insignificant,' but the text says the proposed method is significant at the 95% confidence level for most metrics, and the listed p-values are mostly below 0.05. The title contradicts the content and should be something like 'Two-sample t-test Statistical Significance.'

The annotation description is circular: 'the object point clouds are first upsampled to gain accurate affordance maps using our inference model' and 'Our model then processes the upsampled data to infer accurate affordance maps.' If the OpenHOI model itself is used to produce the affordance annotations used for training/evaluation, those labels are not independent ground truth and can inflate performance.
